title: Vasilisa the Beautiful
text:
When Vasilisa was eight, her mother lay dying. She called the girl to her bed and gave her a tiny wooden doll. "Keep it with you always and show it to no one," she said. "If trouble comes, give it a little food and ask its advice." Then she blessed her daughter and died.

Her father remarried a widow with two daughters, and the three of them were cruel to Vasilisa, piling on work to make her ugly and thin. But each night Vasilisa fed the doll, and the doll comforted her and did her chores while she rested.

One evening the stepmother let every fire and candle in the house go out and sent Vasilisa to the witch Baba Yaga, in the deep forest, to bring back light. Baba Yaga lived in a hut on chicken legs behind a fence of bones. She set the girl impossible tasks: cleaning, cooking, sorting good grain from black. Each night the doll did them.

At last Baba Yaga asked how she managed it all. "My mother's blessing helps me," Vasilisa said. The witch wanted no blessed person in her house. She pushed her out and gave her a skull with burning eyes on a stick to light her way. When Vasilisa reached home, the skull's eyes stared at the stepmother and her daughters and burned them to ashes. Vasilisa later married the tsar.
lesson: What a parent gives in love and teaching can keep guiding a child long after the parent is gone. Pass on blessings that will travel.
people: Vasilisa, her mother, her stepmother and stepsisters, Baba Yaga
source: Alexander Afanasyev, Russian Folk Tales (Narodnye russkie skazki), Vasilisa the Beautiful
